title: Barqūq's majlis: an opinion is asked
dramatic_question: Barqūq presses you for your opinion of another scholar. The record does not say what you answered. What do you say?

situation.when: during Barqūq's reign (784-801/1382-99 in the dissertation; 784-92/1382-90 in Melvin-Koushki's 2016 book); the majlis is undated

invariants.text: According to Ibn Turka's second apology, Sultan Barqūq pressed him in a majlis for his opinion of another scholar, whom Melvin-Koushki identifies as Shams al-Dīn Muḥammad al-Jazarī.
invariants.detail: The identification is Melvin-Koushki's. The apology was written in 1431-32 to Bāysunghur, to seek intercession while his case was unresolved.

invariants.text: Al-Jazarī, originally of Damascus (d. 833/1429 at Herat), later became Ibn Turka's powerful opponent, and his enmity caused Ibn Turka much grief.
The second apology traces al-Jazarī's enmity to Ibn Turka's candid assessment of him to the Mamluk sultan in Egypt.
invariants.detail: This is Ibn Turka's own version of a grievance; Melvin-Koushki gives no corroboration on the pages we hold, and the sources we hold do not say what the assessment was.

prose: You sit in a majlis at Barqūq's court. On Melvin-Koushki's account Akhlāṭī served there as wonderworker, though nothing places him at this majlis. The Sultan presses you, by your own later account, for your opinion of another scholar: Shams al-Dīn Muḥammad al-Jazarī, originally of Damascus, according to Melvin-Koushki.

You will tell this story yourself, in 1431-32, as the start of a feud. It is the only source. It says your assessment was candid, and that al-Jazarī could not name it later in Fars; it does not say whether you praised him or blamed him.

Even the date is loose. Barqūq's reign is given as 1382-99 in Melvin-Koushki's dissertation and as 1382-90 in his later book; on the second dating the majlis would fall before the timeline's arrival in Cairo, about 1393 (our arithmetic).

choices.label: Answer the Sultan frankly: say what you actually think of al-Jazarī's learning, and accept what follows.
costs: In the game, candour costs you al-Jazarī's goodwill. This price is the game's, not the record's.
choices.feedback: The record is silent on what you said. His own later account calls the assessment candid and makes it the source of the feud; that is a self-report to Bāysunghur while he needed help, and Melvin-Koushki gives no corroboration. No choice is marked as the record's here, and the game keeps the one fact that is attested elsewhere: al-Jazarī became a powerful enemy.

choices.label: Praise al-Jazarī warmly, and say nothing that could be repeated against you.
costs: Nothing you said can be quoted against you, so exposure falls. The sultan wanted a judgement and got flattery, and al-Jazarī becomes your enemy anyway. This price is the game's, not the record's.
choices.feedback: The record is silent on what you said, so this is not a counterfactual: nothing says you did not praise him. But al-Jazarī's later enmity is in the sources (attested, medium confidence), and Ibn Turka himself traces it to this hour, so the game does not let praise buy peace.

choices.label: Decline to rank a fellow scholar, and let Akhlāṭī's standing at the Sultan's court cover your refusal.
costs: You lean on the Sayyid, and your name is tied more closely to his circle.
choices.feedback: The record is silent on what you said. No source has Akhlāṭī speak for you, or has you ask him. The only ground for this option is that he was the Sultan's resident alchemist and wonderworker, and a later Shiraz manuscript shows Barqūq giving him gifts. It is open only if you have earned his regard.
